Provide Dedicated pricing estimate and reserved capacity options
Schedule infra deep dive for VPC peering details week of 2026-09-13

Amara Singh: Share existing VPC CIDR ranges, current transit gateway config, and compliance constraints (due 2026-09-12)
Sofia Martinez: Send pricing ballpark for Dedicated + Private deployment (due 2026-09-11)
summary: Discovery call to assess Celestis Finance's requirements for a Private/VPC deployment. Main topics: VPC peering vs PrivateLink, region constraints, egress controls, KMS/HSM integration, SOC2/audit log needs, and pilot sizing. Redwood AE + SE walked through typical deployment patterns and next steps include sharing diagrams, pricing, and scheduling a deeper infra session.
topics: latency vs cost tradeoffs, Dedicated vs Hosted
transcript: [00:00] Sofia Martinez: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. I'm Sofia from Redwood, AE on the account. we've got Ethan and Janelle from our infra team as well.

[00:10] Amara Singh: Hi Sofia, hi team, thanks. I'm Amara, Head of Platform at Celestis Finance. We pulled in Liam and Noah to cover security and networking. PRIYA is on as well, but she said she'll jump in a bit later.

[00:22] Ethan Reed: Great, hi Amara, Liam, Noah. Quick agenda: understand your current infra, constraints for Private/VPC deployment, routing/peering model preferences, KMS needs, and any compliance requirements. then propose options.

[00:34] Liam O'Connor: Sounds good. To start high level — we run a multi-account AWS setup, us-east-1 primary, with some EMEA workloads in eu-west-1. We're sensitive about egress to public internet and prefer private endpoints for anything that touches PII. we also use a transit gateway for some cross-account routing.

[00:48] Janelle Park: Understood. Typical path here is Redwood Private in a customer VPC or a VPC peering+PrivateLink model. quick Q: are you open to peering between our managed VPC and your account, or do you require a fully customer-hosted deployment inside your VPCs?

[01:02] Amara Singh: For initial pilot we prefer our VPC to host endpoints, but long term we might consider peering if that gives us better manageability. compliance will want all data flows to be auditable and no egress to third-party public internet without logging.

[01:18] Noah Patel: Also, any solution must support our KMS key policies; we rotate keys regularly and need proof that Redwood supports customer-managed keys/HSM and can integrate with our KMS for encrypting persisted caches.

[01:30] Ethan Reed: Yep, Redwood Private supports both customer-managed KMS and HSM-backed keys — integration is typically via cross-account IAM roles and key grant. we'll document the key flow. there can be some gotchas with key policies and cross-account decrypt, we'll share examples.

[01:44] Priya Desai: Sorry for the slight delay. quick question on latency: if we run model inference in eu-west-1 for a subset of traffic but most seats are still in us-east-1, what's the routing fallback? do we get automatic region routing, or would that cause cross-region egress?

[01:58] Janelle Park: Good question. Redwood has smart routing — requests are routed by policy. for Private, we can deploy nodes in both regions and route traffic by client IP or by route table. if only us-east-1 is available and you call eu-west-1 endpoint, that will be cross-region and you pay egress as usual. we recommend pinning region per workload to avoid cross-region latency and egress costs.

[02:18] Liam O'Connor: OK. about networking models — we prefer not to open public endpoints at all. can you explain peering vs PrivateLink for this use case? we've had issues with peering and overlapping CIDRs.

[02:30] Ethan Reed: Sure. VPC peering is a straight L3 route — it's simple but requires non-overlapping CIDRs and doesn't support transitive routing via TGW unless you use transit gateway attachments. PrivateLink (AWS PrivateLink) exposes a Network Load Balancer endpoint in your VPC as an interface endpoint — it's more scalable across accounts and avoids CIDR overlap problems, but it requires ENIs and private DNS entries. Both are supported by Redwood; choice often depends on your network design and CIDR constraints.
[02:53] Amara Singh: We use a transit gateway for several account connections. Would Redwood integrate with a TGW or do we need direct peering?

[03:03] Janelle Park: We can do TGW attachments on a case-by-case basis. for larger enterprise deployments we typically provision a managed VPC and attach it to your TGW, or we can deploy in your account behind PrivateLink. each has tradeoffs: TGW gives full routing but requires more network ops coordination; PrivateLink is simpler to consume from many accounts.

[03:18] Noah Patel: How about egress to S3 for model artifacts and cache persistence? our policy mandates VPC endpoints for S3 — will your deployment support S3 VPC endpoints so data never traverses the public internet?

[03:29] Ethan Reed: Absolutely. We support VPC endpoints for S3 and recommend configuring S3 gateway endpoints or VPC endpoint policies. For model pulls, if you keep artifacts in your account, you can restrict access with bucket policies referencing the VPC endpoint. we can provide an example policy.

[03:43] Liam O'Connor: On the security front — SOC2 and audit logs. we need to show auditors that request logs exist, who accessed what, and that logs are immutable. what's Redwood's approach to audit logs and retention?

[03:54] Sofia Martinez: Redwood Console provides per-route and per-model tracing and audit logs; for Private deployments we ship logs to a customer-controlled S3 bucket or to your logging endpoint. retention and immutability can be handled via S3 object lock or by forwarding to your SIEM (Splunk/Datadog). we'll surface the relevant logs for the SOC2 report.
[04:14] Priya Desai: Nice. about compute sizing: what are the typical CPU/GPU footprints for a pilot? we want to estimate cost and throughput — our initial pilot is light, maybe 10 qps bursty.

[04:26] Janelle Park: For small pilot, a few GPUs or even CPU-backed instances with quantized models might be enough for low-throughput evaluation. if you need low latency for customer-facing flows, Dedicated GPU pools are preferred. we'll need a sample workload to give tighter numbers, but we can provide ballpark throughput for common models.
[04:40] Amara Singh: We're leaning to start in Private with a small footprint in our VPC to meet compliance, then decide on Dedicated if performance needs increase. cost sensitivity is high though.

[04:50] Ethan Reed: Totally. There's also caching and prefix KV cache that can reduce tokens served and costs. for you, we'd recommend enabling KV caches and prefix caching where possible to lower per-token costs; these are configurable in Redwood Private.

[05:02] Liam O'Connor: One more networking nit — NAT gateways. we try to minimize NAT egress. if Redwood nodes need to pull updates or contact registries, will that require our NAT or can it be staged through internal endpoints?

[05:13] Janelle Park: We can arrange model staging using your S3 buckets or a private artifact repository. for orchestrator heartbeats, most traffic can be over private endpoints. we'll detail the required outbound connections; the goal is to avoid unnecessary NAT egress.

[05:25] Sofia Martinez: Quick note — we've seen customers block public egress entirely and operate successfully, as long as you provide required endpoints (S3, KMS, and Redwood control plane endpoints if you opt to keep a control plane in our tenancy). we can also offer a private control plane for full isolation.
[05:40] Priya Desai: Private control plane — can you explain the difference versus customer-hosted control plane? what are the management responsibilities?

[05:48] Ethan Reed: Private control plane is where Redwood runs control plane components in a customer-dedicated account or in our managed environment with private connectivity; customer-hosted means we deliver software you install in your account. Private control plane reduces ops burden but still keeps network boundaries private. install-in-your-account gives you max isolation but requires more ops.
[06:06] Amara Singh: For compliance we prefer either private control plane in our AWS tenancy or a full customer-hosted install. can you share docs on the install requirements?
[06:14] Sofia Martinez: Yes — we'll send the deployment checklist and Terraform examples. Ethan will lead on networking specifics.
[06:21] Liam O'Connor: On encryption at rest — you mentioned KV cache and model weights. if we use customer-managed KMS, do you encrypt only storage or also in-memory caches?

[06:32] Janelle Park: KMS covers persisted storage. in-memory caches are ephemeral; for more sensitive data we can configure not to persist it. if you need HSM-backed encryption for persisted caches, we support HSM KMS providers in the key life cycle.
[06:46] Noah Patel: We also need SSO/SAML integration for admin access and RBAC. can admin console access be federated to our IdP and audit admin actions?
[06:57] Ethan Reed: Yes, Redwood supports SAML SSO and fine-grained RBAC. for Private we can integrate with your IdP and push admin audit events to your logging sink.

[07:09] Priya Desai: There was a brief mention of model quantization recommendations — how does Redwood handle different model variants across regions? We need to ensure consistent quality if we run 8-bit in one region and 16-bit in another.

[07:21] Janelle Park: Good point. We surface model and quantization profiles in the console and can pin routes to model variants. if you want consistent quality we recommend pinning the same variant and running A/B evals to monitor regressions. Redwood Optimize can suggest quantization profiles by workload.
[07:36] Amara Singh: Let's talk about timeline and stakeholders. We'll need security sign-off and infra sign-off. target is to have pilot by end of October; is that reasonable?

[07:46] Sofia Martinez: Absolutely reasonable. next steps from our side: share network diagram and whitepaper, provide a pricing ballpark, and schedule the infra deep dive. From your side: share CIDRs, transit gateway details, and KMS policies.
[07:58] Liam O'Connor: Also, can you run a short benchmark from our network to a Redwood Private endpoint to validate latency? we'd like to see p50/p95 numbers for sample prompts.

[08:08] Ethan Reed: Yes, we can run a controlled benchmark. we'll need a small script and maybe a set of sample prompts; we can coordinate during the infra deep dive. note that numbers vary by model and instance type.

[08:20] Priya Desai: On the legal/compliance side — log retention, data deletion, and breach notification timelines — we need these in writing for procurement. can you share the SOC2 and data processing addendum?
[08:31] Sofia Martinez: We'll share SOC2 attestation and DPA. for breach notification and retention, we'll provide standard language and are open to negotiated terms for enterprise contracts.
[08:44] Amara Singh: Are there any known limitations or gotchas customers hit during Private installs that we should be aware of?

[08:51] Janelle Park: The common ones: overlapping CIDRs blocking peering, KMS key policy misconfigurations preventing decrypts, and missing endpoint policies for S3 which cause model pulls to fail. those are solvable but we've seen them in initial installs.
[09:05] Noah Patel: Good to know. about monitoring — can we attach Datadog metrics from the Redwood runtime or do we ingest logs only?

[09:15] Ethan Reed: We export metrics and traces; Datadog integration is supported via a forwarder or direct metric export depending on deployment. logs can go to your SIEM and we can also send metrics to a Prometheus endpoint if you prefer.
[09:27] Amara Singh: Question on billing — with Private deployments is billing via Redwood contract or can we be invoiced to our procurement if we manage underlying infra costs ourselves?

[09:36] Sofia Martinez: Typically software/SLAs are invoiced by Redwood, infra costs (if in your account) remain with you. for Dedicated reserved pools we have commit pricing and can structure invoices to match procurement needs.
[09:48] Liam O'Connor: On firewall rules — do you need specific ports open inbound to our VPC? we try to minimize inbound allowances.

[09:56] Janelle Park: For PrivateLink the traffic is initiated from inside your VPC to the interface endpoint so inbound rules are minimal; for peering/TGW you need appropriate route table entries but not broadly open ports. we'll provide the minimal port list.
[10:09] Priya Desai: If we decide to scale later with Dedicated GPU pools, can we keep the same VPC/networking config or will we need a migration?

[10:18] Ethan Reed: We design the migration to be seamless: model endpoints and routes can be remapped. there's some operational work but no heavy data migration — caches can be warmed. it's a common pattern: start Private in your VPC, migrate heavy traffic to Dedicated while keeping control plane visibility.
[10:32] Amara Singh: Perfect. Any requirements for our side to rotate keys or can Redwood manage rotation with our policies?

[10:40] Janelle Park: We recommend customer-managed rotation via your KMS; Redwood can rotate keys on your schedule if given permissions, but best practice is letting the customer control rotation and we use grants for access.
[10:52] Liam O'Connor: A quick call-out — we use IP whitelisting for some services. can Redwood support static IP egress so we can whitelist IPs for our outbound firewall?
[11:02] Ethan Reed: For managed deployments we can provide a set of egress IPs; for fully customer-hosted installs egress IPs come from your NAT config. we'll document the options.
[11:12] Sofia Martinez: We're coming up on the 30-minute mark; should we go deeper on any of these or open for questions?
[11:18] Noah Patel: I'd like to dig into PrivateLink specifics and DNS resolution nuances, maybe in the infra deep dive.
[11:24] Amara Singh: Same, please. also want the sample Terraform so our infra team can review.

[11:30] Ethan Reed: We'll prepare a Terraform snippet showing a PrivateLink endpoint service, the interface endpoint config, and example endpoint policy. that should help with DNS and route53 private zones.
[11:42] Priya Desai: One more — do you support bringing your own model artifacts or only Redwood-curated models?

[11:49] Janelle Park: You can bring-your-own models. for Private we allow loading artifacts from your S3 and we can register those as model variants; we just need access patterns and IAM roles defined.
[11:58] Liam O'Connor: Good. about certificate management for TLS on private endpoints — do you manage certs or do we provide them?

[12:06] Ethan Reed: For PrivateLink the interface endpoints use AWS private DNS and TLS is handled by NLB certs; we can either manage certs or you can supply ACM certs in your account if you prefer full control.
[12:16] Amara Singh: Ok, let's summarize next steps and owners so procurement and security know what's coming.

[12:24] Sofia Martinez: Summary — Redwood to send: 1) private deployment network diagram and whitepaper (Sofia/Ethan), 2) Terraform/PrivateLink example (Ethan), 3) SOC2 + DPA + security docs (Sofia), 4) pricing ballpark (Sofia). Customer to send: CIDR ranges, TGW topology, KMS policies (Amara/Liam). We'll schedule infra deep dive for next week.
[12:48] Amara Singh: That works. any blockers on our side that would prevent a pilot by end of October? we need to know now so procurement timelines can be adjusted.
[12:58] Sofia Martinez: None from our side. as long as we get the CIDRs and KMS policies this week and confirm a small pilot scope, we can start provisioning next week.
[13:09] Noah Patel: Great. last question — can you provide an example of audit logs format so our auditors can see the schema?
[13:16] Janelle Park: We'll attach sample log exports — JSON lines with request_id, model, route, timestamp, user_id, and token counts. also show how we forward to S3 or your SIEM.
[13:27] Priya Desai: Thanks all. that covers most of it for now.
[13:31] Sofia Martinez: Thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the docs and a proposed time for the deep dive. cheers.
[13:35] Call ended
